en: When I read the writing,
My leopard mother's name is there.
My precious, fierce mother's
Keng-Kolchuk from her girlhood,
Surrounded by a grove of plane trees,
With pools all around,
A black, white-blazed thoroughbred
She would ride in splendor.
Ninety girls followed her.
My poor mother Kanykey,
In her girlhood then,
Would come on pilgrimage.
On its plane tree, this very year,
A nightingale has flown down and perched.
Its poplars have leafed out, their branches full;
My godlike father Manas
Seems still to be alive.”
The boy prepared to take the road,
To Manas, gone to the next world,
Your boy pleaded with his spirit.
Kanykey had come in mourning;
When he was a nursing infant,
Semetey had fled here.
The orphan had come to Bukhara and grown.
To Khan Temir's city
He had wandered, keeping himself alive.
When they came to Khan Temir,
His ill-fated mother,
The prince's only son,
Snipping his little twig,
For this khan of Bukhara
Had performed the ritual.
The orphan grew to maturity,
And thus joined the ranks,
Growing up, becoming a hero,
Without deviation from Manas,
A hero exactly like him.
When he reached Keng-Kolchuk,
He adjusted his winged steed's saddle.
To Manas, gone to the next world,
He dedicated a recitation of the Quran.
When the boy was in Bukhara,
In the woods he heard words from Taz;
He heard that his people were Kyrgyz,
That his horse was white-blazed,
That his father was someone else,
That Akynkhan and the Afghans were his in-laws,
That Aichurok was his wife,
Saying a holy sage had given his blessing,
That he followed twelve spiritual masters—
Mighty Sultan Khan Manas—
'He is your father,' he said.
'Talas is your land,' he said.
'The Kyrgyz are your people,' he said.
The son of a prince—
What reason had he to wander as a fugitive?
Where were his poor Kyrgyz people?
To the land left by his father,
Semetey was going,
To those Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
His father Khan Manas came into his thoughts.
The orphan servant left by my Khan Manas,
Aktulpar beneath him,
He lashed his whip on either side,
Spurring to right and left.
The orphan set his course and traveled,
Going far, not sparing his horse.
As the sun wavered toward setting,
Kulesheng's Kul-Tokoy—
He reached Kul-Tokoy.
Kulesheng's Kul-Tokoy,
Lay spread out luxuriantly,
Its yellow valley stretching proudly.
Apples ripened and fell to mulch;
It was a land loved by God.
Walnuts fell and filled the ravines.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoy
Had all its wealth in perfect order.
Its little birds were like snowcocks;
Its plane trees stood like towers.
Its mountains held snow;
Its forest held rooks.
Every living creature was there.
Its hogweed stems were thick as forearms;
Its red deer, when urged on,
Were like pale, white-blazed cows.
There were foxes on its plains,
Argali on its foothills,
Deer on its hillocks,
Nightingales in its plane trees.
When its nightingales warbled,
A sorrowful person could not bear to hear;
If the grieving gathered there sobbing,
A sorrowful person could not leave.
Its parrots spread their wings;
Owls spoke from its mountains.
Kul-Tokoy was a splendid place.
Its birds laid eggs in the birches,
Preparing to fly;
Its birds laid eggs in the poplars,
Straining to fly.
It had marshes here and there;
It was a wooded upland pasture set apart.
Your fierce mother Kanykey,
When she fled Bukhara on foot,
My noble-horse father Khan Manas's treasure,
When the foolish ones scattered it,
For a woman whose husband had died,
Thinking her birth family would be near,
Suffering hardship without a way out,
When my mother fled Talas on foot,
When she came to Kul-Tokoy,
When my wretched mother suffered humiliation,
The old woman coughed on her back.
The old woman and her child
My mother carried, straining.
My poor mother Kanykey
Stepped on, swaying along.
My poor, wretched mother's
Blood streamed from her calves;
The flesh of her soles was gouged away,
And from all her heels
The skin was stripped, leaving none intact.
Her dark thighs swelled soft,
Waterlogged like leather skins.
The two women, tired and weeping,
Sobbed and cried aloud.
Me, in my swaddling clothes,
My mother kept safe in one place.
Pure white milk flowed from the plane tree,
Enveloping my mother.
Food appeared from the unseen world.
Me, the orphan, my God
Saved in this way.
At the plane tree where his mother had lain,
Aktulpar beneath him,
He removed its saddle, leaving it barebacked.
He tethered it to the plane tree,
Fastening it securely by one foreleg.
Pillowing his head upon the white saddle,
That dear child born of Manas
Lay with his head toward Mecca.
Spreading the blue saddlecloth,
Praying to the one God,
Pillowing his head upon his sharp sword,
Your poor one left by Manas,
Dipped his hands in the water,
And performed his hand ablution.
That unyielding warrior lay motionless,
Praying to the one God,
Not drawing back his outstretched legs,
Not opening his closed eyes.
The dear lion left by Manas,
That proud, cock-like hero,
Fell into a giant's sleep.
Taking a short rest in sleep,
His father, fierce Manas,
That dear one was born to surpass.
Your goshawk left by his father Manas,
When dawn spread bright,
When light fell upon the earth,
When the Scales constellation set,
When dawn broke clear,
Awoke with a start from sleep.
Turning like a lion,
Dipping his hands in the water,
To his departed father Manas's
Spirit he prayed.
“It is God's commanded duty,” he said,
Preparing for prayer.
Two cycles of the dawn prayer
He managed to recite.
“Amen!” he said, spreading his hands.
As he recited his prayer,
When he looked at Aktulpar,
Its head resting toward his feet,
Its head turned toward Mecca,
It had no tongue to speak;
That dear beast, wiser than other animals—
Aktulpar and Semetey,
The two lay foot to foot,
Having slept together.
Quickly saying his prayers,
The orphan servant left by Manas
Saddled Aktulpar.
Again the orphan took the road,
Traveling far, not sparing his horse.
The misty, saddle-shaped ridge
Was the pass of Aman-Zhol his mother had crossed.
With their ears pricked,
Wolves did not roam there;
With their tails trailing,
Foxes did not roam there.
My poor mother Kanykey,
The road she trotted like a hunting hound,
Suffering privation and real hardship,
Wandering tirelessly on foot,
Her soles battered by stones,
Her forehead scorched by the hot sun—
Aman-Zhol, by which my mother came.
These were my dear mother's words;
'This is Aman-Zhol,' she said.
Semetey turned aside,
Not passing peacefully along Aman-Zhol,
Not leaving quietly without stirring trouble.
He went down through the jutting hollow,
Crossed the mountain spur hanging before him.
When he reached the overhanging mountain,
That tireless hero,
When he climbed its back,
And set his course along the ridge—
Let me tell of the valiant one's plight:
At the sight his attention was drawn.
Shrouded in haze, rising in corners,
Low mist settled around its jutting edges,
Dark smoke rose apart.
My mother's precious words—
There was Kokand, looming dark.
It was Kokand itself.
The orphan boy grew excited;
He had reached Kokand.
These were my mother's words:
'If you can, by Kokand,
My only one, pass without approaching,' she said.
The reason not to approach was this:
When my holy father lived,
He used to humiliate Kokand,
Six thousand silver ingots and a thousand otter pelts
He used to take in tribute.
If they did not pay that tribute,
If they would not obey his words,
My father did as he pleased.
Loading elephants, taking gold coins,
If his anger once took hold,
He took a thousand dark-eyed people.
When he wrought havoc among the Sarts,
He plundered their valuables.
He truly wrought destruction;
Unable to endure that suffering,
Many of them were left weeping.
These were my mother's words:
'The high official in Kokand
Has a grudge against your father Khan Manas;
He will be hostile toward you,' she said.
'He will be less inclined to reconciliation,' she said.
“When I go to the khan of Kokand,
Let me not fall needlessly into disaster.
In a Sart's house in Kokand,
There is grain beer kept in a leather bucket.
If he serves food while singing his song,
There is burning poison mixed in.
There is grain beer brewed from millet,
With a weakening poison mixed inside.
In the khan of Kokand's palace,
Beneath a gold-patterned carpet,
Dug underneath,
